checklist.evidence: The draft says CSS has a native `token()` function in every current browser. No such CSS function exists. The CSS custom properties, WCAG 4.5:1 and DTCG 2025.10 statements are correct.
Practical and friendly. No hype, no vendor comparison, no invented personal experience.
Covers why small teams benefit, when to adopt, common mistakes and a React + CSS variables example. The must_include code example is present but invalid (see i2).
The `token()` browser-support claim has no source and is contradicted by the CSS specs and MDN.
Audience inferred as community (front-end leads who are peers). The register is peer-level and the cost reasoning is concrete.
The title promises why small teams should adopt tokens. The intro sets up the forty-file problem and that exact question.
Title, intro (a relatable green-hex story) and conclusion form one arc. A skimmer gets the point.
The conclusion calls back to the forty-file green search and closes with the one-line-edit idea. It is partly a recap, but the callback holds.
Sentences are short and clean. I found no run-ons, comma splices or stray capitals.

The CSS block uses `$color-primary: ...` declarations and `token(color-primary)`, which are not valid CSS. The prose says `--` prefix and `var()`, and the React snippet uses `var(--color-surface)`. The CSS and React samples contradict each other, and the CSS one does not run.
No flagged words and 0 em dashes found. The phrasing is plain.
The FAQ has 5 genuine next questions, headings are descriptive and sentence case, and a clear claim sits in the intro. A TLDR is not needed at about 900 words.
The reference page is MDN's 'Using CSS custom properties'. The article adds a cost-per-use adoption heuristic and a mistakes list. It offers no hands-on failure or measured result.
The quotable insight is 'The repeat count and the planned changes decide the payoff, not the size of the company.' It is reasoning-based and reasonably sharp but thin.
The reader leaves with clear adoption triggers (repeating values, planned theming, naming disputes), a start-small path and a mistakes list.
V1: about 3 instances. V2: about 2 instances. Several lines open on the problem or the negative. See i4.
V3: no meaningful passives. The few passive-ish constructions are justified.

issues.anchor: CSS now has a native `token()` function in every current browser, so no `var()` is needed:
issues.description: There is no native CSS `token()` function. Custom properties are read with `var()`, as the draft's own MDN claim says. This is an invented API stated as universal browser support, with no source. Delete the sentence and the `token()` usage. Use `var(--color-primary)`.

The CSS sample declares properties with a Sass-style `$` prefix and reads them with the nonexistent `token()`, so it will not run. The prose and the React snippet use `--name` and `var(--name)`. Rewrite it as `--color-primary: #0a5c36;` inside `:root`, `[data-theme="dark"] { --color-surface: #14181c; }`, and `.button { background: var(--color-primary); padding: var(--space-2) var(--space-4); }`.

issues.anchor: The repeat count and the planned changes decide the payoff, not the size of the company.
issues.description: The adoption heuristic is a useful angle, but it stays abstract. The article could add a concrete trade-off the docs omit, for example what a small team should do about the `blue-500` naming layer or a worked rebrand edit count. Build it from reasoning and verified sources, not invented experience.

issues.anchor: Small teams hit the same wall, and nobody on the team has the job of catching it.
issues.description: Problem-first and negative framings. Other examples: the bullet label 'Ignoring the cost.' and 'Instead of writing `#0a5c36` in forty places'. Lead with the gain, for example 'Small teams get the same payoff, and a shared file gives everyone one place to catch it.' Rename the bullet to 'Plan for the indirection.'
The DTCG stable-version claim cites an announcement URL in the front matter, but the References list links only the group's landing page. Link the announcement post in the text or References.

technical_accuracy.evidence: The invented `token()` function and the `$` syntax are wrong. The core CSS variable, WCAG and DTCG statements are accurate.

technical_depth.evidence: Covers the cascade, theming, the invalid-at-computed-value-time behavior and when to add a build step. It stays introductory.

practical_usefulness.evidence: Adoption triggers and the mistakes list are applicable. The primary code example would mislead a reader who copies it.

originality.evidence: The cost-per-use adoption reasoning and the misconception angle are present. The rest is standard guidance.

structure_clarity.evidence: The flow runs from problem to concept to code to when to adopt, then mistakes, trade-offs and FAQ. Headings are clear.

examples_implementation.evidence: The CSS sample is invalid and contradicts the React sample. The React snippet itself is fine.

tradeoffs_limitations.evidence: Covers runtime resolution, no compile-time typo detection, indirection cost and when to wait.

references_support.evidence: MDN, DTCG and WCAG are real and relevant. The token() claim is unsupported.

seo.evidence: The primary keyword is in the title, intro and headings. The description is good, and secondary terms appear.

audience_fit.evidence: The tone suits front-end leads at small teams, with a practical, friendly register.

factual_correctness.evidence: The claim that CSS has a native `token()` function in all current browsers is false, and the CSS sample built on it is invalid.

claim_checks.claim: CSS custom properties are declared with a -- prefix and read with var(), and they cascade and inherit
CSS now has a native `token()` function in every current browser, so no `var()` is needed
claim_checks.evidence: No `token()` function exists in the CSS specs or MDN. Custom properties use `var()`.

claim_checks.claim: The W3C Design Tokens Community Group published the first stable version (2025.10) of its format in October 2025; it is a Community Group specification, not a W3C Standard
claim_checks.evidence: The group announced the stable 2025.10 spec on 28 October 2025. It is a Community Group report, not a W3C Recommendation. I recalled this and did not re-fetch it.

claim_checks.claim: WCAG minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for body text
claim_checks.evidence: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1 for normal text.

claim_checks.claim: A var() pointing at an undefined property is invalid at computed-value time and the browser falls back to the inherited or initial value
claim_checks.evidence: This matches the CSS Variables spec behavior for invalid-at-computed-value-time declarations.

summary: Gate: the article is worth writing because forty-file hex hunts hit small teams too, and it earns the read through a relatable opening and a concrete adoption heuristic. Scorecard: audience pass, title pass, skim pass, conclusion pass, sentences pass, code fail (invalid `$` and `token()` syntax), words pass, fact-check fail (invented `token()` API), humans/machines pass, beats docs flag, originality flag, so what pass, V1/V2 flag, V3 pass.
